name: Simple CEA/BOTEC of CHAI TSUs, April 2025
summary: Funds technical support units that help governments, such as Malawi's and Burkina Faso's, spend their health budgets better. GiveWell's spreadsheet "Simple CEA/BOTEC of CHAI TSUs, April 2025", linked from 2 of its grant pages. Every number is traced from the sheet's bottom line; calculated rows reproduce the sheet's own values.

rows.label: % improvement in cost-effectivess of government health spending due to allocative efficiencies (Malawi)
rows.explainer: We benchmark this to the 20% improvement to cost-effectiveness that we believe CHAI's GiveWell-funded PPM (Program Performance Management) team can achieve for internal programs. Whilst we believe there may be more room for improvement in the average government program (compared to the average CHAI program), we also think that the cost-effectiveness lense will be weighted less highly in decision making given other government priorities. See the rationale for this PPM grant we made to CHAI in October 2024.

rows.explainer:
We believe that the benefits of the TSU's work will continue for a little longer than the grant period itself (6 months beyond the one-year grant period, so benefits over a total of 1.5 years). These additional benefits could come from a few channels, such as continued effects on government decision-making after the TSU stops working with the government, or the expenditure the TSU influences last for beyond the one year.

In our view these years are discounted at the shared rate (Discount rate on the years of benefit); the evaluator view counts them at face value.

rows.label: Discount rate on the years of benefit
rows.explainer: Changed for consistency. GiveWell's sheet adds up the years a benefit lasts at face value here, so a benefit in a later year counts as much as one now. The site discounts every future benefit at one shared rate (Next year's good counts less by, under Your values): each year counted here is worth (1 + rate)^-t of a year now, the first one in full. The evaluator view keeps no discounting.

rows.label: Units of value per dollar from Give Directly's direct cash transfer program (Burkina Faso)
rows.explainer: Calculated in GiveWell's cost-effectiveness analysis of GiveDirectly. Changed for consistency: GiveWell's sheet used 0.0034 units of value per dollar given to GiveDirectly here. The site values cash with one shared benchmark for every model (The cash benchmark, under Data), the same figure that turns this model's multiple of cash back into units of value: where the sheet divides by it to make its multiple, the benchmark cancels in our view, so our units of value are the sheet's before it divided by cash. The evaluator view keeps 0.0034.

rows.label: Cost-effectiveness of TSU (in multiples of Give Directly's cost-efectiveness, "x cash") (Burkina Faso)
Units of value per dollar given to GiveDirectly
rows.explainer: GiveWell reports this model's result in multiples of cash transfers. Multiplying by GiveWell's value of a dollar to GiveDirectly converts it into units of value per dollar, so it ranks against the other models. Older sheets used older moral weights; the multiple of cash is the comparable number across years. It is the site's shared cash benchmark (The cash benchmark, under Data), the one figure every model's multiple of cash is turned into units of value with.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: Default for research, technical assistance and policy work: mostly people. Our judgment; we haven't seen this grant's breakdown.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: Researchers and advisers could typically earn considerably more in consulting or industry. Our judgment.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff per dollar of cost (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid in cash
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of the cost, and staff get their share of the outcome. Off, this is 100%.

rows.label: Units of value per dollar
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, times the share of the full cost paid in cash (staff's forgone pay is the rest).
